A game console made of neurons

Snake, played on a tiny computer whose every clock tick is one neural network. Pure CSS, with 0 bytes of JavaScript.

  • The console: a small 8-bit computer with 90 bytes of memory. The 8 × 8 screen is part of that memory: whatever the program writes there is what you see.
  • One tick, one network: 676 neurons read the next instruction, do it, and move on. Each of your moves runs 36 ticks of the game: move the head, eat, grow, put down new food, check for crashes.
  • The game is a program: 42 instructions in the console's own little language. The network knows nothing about Snake: give it another program and it plays another game.
  • Try: steer with the arrows. The snake's head is the bright square with the pale rim. Eat the red dots, don't hit the wall or your own tail. You have 60 moves.

How it works (for the curious)

The console's instructions

Two 8-bit registers, A and B, a program counter, and 90 bytes of memory. The cartridge is 48 instructions, each a code and a number (n a number, m a memory cell, t an instruction). Numbers wrap around at 256, memory cells at 90.

WAITstop here for goodADD mA = A + memory[m]
SYNC twait for the next button, then go on at tSUB mA = A − memory[m]
LDI nA = nADDI nA = A + n
LD mA = memory[m]WRAP nif A ≥ n: A = A − n
ST mmemory[m] = ANEXT nB = B + n (around the 90 cells)
LDX nA = memory[B + n]JMP tgo to t
STX nmemory[B + n] = AJZ tgo to t if A is 0
SETX nmemory[B] = nJNZ tgo to t if A is not 0
LDB mB = memory[m]JXNZ tgo to t if memory[B] is not 0
TABB = AINA = the button pressed (1 to 4)
TBAA = Bother codes do nothing

The memory is the screen

A 9 × 10 grid: the 8 × 8 playfield and a wall around it (the left and right walls share one column). The snake only needs the wall to be "not empty", so wall cells also hold the game's variables. An empty cell is 0, the wall 1, food 2, the head 3, and a body cell holds the address of the next piece towards the head: moving the tail is one lookup. New food goes 23 cells further on, then further again while that cell is taken.

One tick, as ReLUs

PartHow
fetch[PC = i] for every line, each gating that line's code and number: relu(op_i − 31·(1 − [PC = i]) − 31·waiting)
decode[op = k] for each code, from one shared row of units relu(op − k + 1)
addressm, B + n or B, each mod 90 with one unit: ⌊x / 90⌋ = round(relu(2x − 89) / 180)
memoryevery cell read through [address = j]; the written cell becomes cell − relu(cell − 255·h) + relu(data − 255·h), h = 2 − [address = j] − write
conditionsfolded into the gates: relu(x − 47·(1 − JXNZ) − 47·memory[B]) is "x if JXNZ and the cell is empty": with x the next line it falls through, and subtracted from t it jumps when the cell is not empty

One tick is 676 units. The page writes 12 ticks out as one network of 8,112 units and 51,575 weights, and runs it 3 times per move: 24,336 units per click. As a strict layered network one tick is 11 layers and 1,730 units, most of them only passing values down a layer (grey below). In CSS every unit of a step sits on the same element and can read any other directly, so the page leaves those out.

A move whose buttons haven't been pressed yet is hidden, so the browser computes nothing inside it: a click computes just that move's 36 ticks. Browsers stop nesting HTML at 512 levels; 12 ticks per network keeps the 60 moves at 360 levels.

Checked

A plain Python emulator runs the console, and a plain Python Snake checks the emulator: 5,000 games, every move. The networks match the emulator in numpy, every register and memory cell: one tick, every tick, on 3,000 random programs and 100 games; the 12-tick network after every step, on 2,000 random programs and 300 full games. Every partial sum, measured on every state of those runs, stays below 224 by a factor of more than 100, so 32-bit CSS engines are exact too. The browser test plays 12 games by clicking the arrows in Chromium, Firefox and WebKit and compares the screen, score and game over after every move.
